title: The Threshold of Clocks
story:
A smile on a stranger could mean many things. A smile could mean a trick, hidden behind teeth. A smile could mean a challenge, issued in silence. But this smile, wrinkling the corners of the old man’s eyes as James finished the sweet apple slice, meant only welcome. Barnaby stood up slowly, his knees making a soft popping sound that reminded James of dry twigs snapping underfoot in the Great Canopy. He gestured toward a low wooden door at the end of the alleyway, a door bathed in the same golden lantern light. He did not rush James, nor did he reach out to grab him; he simply walked to the door, held it open, and waited.

James hesitated, looking back once at the dark alley and the drain where his metal ring had vanished. Then, taking a deep breath of the cold air, he took his first steps across the threshold. Here was a room of quiet ticking clocks. Here was a room of curled paper maps. Here was a room of brass instruments that smelled faintly of the same oil he had smelled on the wind. It was warm, heated by a small brick fireplace where orange embers pulsed like sleepy fireflies.

Barnaby pulled up a small wooden stool near the hearth, indicating James should sit, and laid a large sheet of thick paper on the table. With gentle, weathered hands, the old man took a piece of charcoal and drew a simple, beautiful map. He drew the Great Canopy, the Whispering Flats, the wire fence, and finally, a tiny monkey shape sitting inside a small house. He handed a small, broken stub of the charcoal to James, nodding encouragingly. For the first time since leaving the trees, James felt the vastness of the world shrink into something safe, watching the embers glow as he held his new drawing tool.
